text: What runs around the whole yard without moving, and is alive?
why_original_fails: A fence is not alive; a hedge is and surrounds a yard.
original_text: What runs around the whole yard without moving?

jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.final: A hedge — a living row of shrubs around the yard
jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.label: correct

text: What can fill a room but takes up no space, and you hear it?
why_original_fails: Light is seen, not heard; sound fills a room and takes no space.
original_text: What can fill a room but takes up no space?

text: What goes through cities and fields, never moves, and carries electricity?
why_original_fails: A road carries no electricity; power lines cross cities and fields and do.
original_text: What goes through cities and fields but never moves?

text: What kind of band never plays music, and holds your watch on your wrist?
why_original_fails: A rubber band does not hold a watch; a watch band does.
original_text: What kind of band never plays music?

text: Something walks on four legs in the morning, two legs at noon, and three legs in the evening. What is the third leg in the evening?
why_original_fails: The question asks about the third leg, the old person's cane, not what the creature is.
original_text: What walks on four legs in the morning, two legs at noon, and three legs in the evening?

text: A piano has keys but can't open locks. What has locks but no keys, and grows on your head?
why_original_fails: The question asks for something with locks that grows on your head, which is hair; 'piano' is stated as the thing with keys.
original_text: What has keys but can't open locks?

text: If a hen lays an egg on top of a barn roof that slopes down to the west, which way does the egg roll?
why_original_fails: A hen does lay eggs, so the trick is gone; the egg rolls down the stated slope, to the west.
original_text: If a rooster lays an egg on top of a barn roof, which way does the egg roll?

text: Two mothers and two daughters went out to eat. Everyone ate one burger, and four burgers were eaten in total. How many people went out to eat?
why_original_fails: Four burgers, one each, means four people; the three-generation trick applies to three burgers.
original_text: Two mothers and two daughters went out to eat. Everyone ate one burger, yet only three burgers were eaten in total. How is this possible?
original_answer: they are a grandmother, a mother and a daughter

text: Which is grammatically correct: "the yolk of the egg is yellow" or "the yolk of the egg are yellow"?
answer: the yolk of the egg is yellow
why_original_fails: Yolks are yellow, so the color trap is gone; only the grammar question remains, and 'is' is correct.
original_text: Which is correct: "the yolk of the egg is white" or "the yolk of the egg are white"?

text: What do you throw out to use and take in when you're done, and it has a baited hook at the end?
why_original_fails: An anchor carries no baited hook; a fishing line is cast out, reeled in, and ends in a baited hook.
original_text: What do you throw out to use and take in when you're done?

text: I have a neck but no head. I have a body but no arms. I have a bottom but no legs. I make music when my strings are plucked. What am I?
why_original_fails: A bottle has no strings; a guitar has a neck, a body, a bottom and strings.
original_text: I have a neck but no head. I have a body but no arm. I have a bottom but no leg.

text: I am so simple that I can only point, yet I guide people all over the world, and I am part of your hand. What am I?
why_original_fails: A compass is not part of a hand; a finger is and points.
original_text: I am so simple that I can only point. Yet I guide men all over the world.

text: You throw away the outside and cook the inside. Then you eat the outside and throw away the inside. What did you throw away last?
why_original_fails: The question asks what was thrown away last, the cob; 'corn' is what was eaten.
original_text: You throw away the outside and cook the inside. Then you eat the outside and throw away the inside. What did you eat?

text: What has six faces but no eyes, and every face is a square?
why_original_fails: A die has twenty-one 'eyes'; a plain cube has six square faces and none.
original_text: What has six faces and twenty-one eyes?

text: What is that over the head and under the hat, on a completely bald man?
why_original_fails: A bald man has no hair; what is under his hat is bare scalp, or nothing.
original_text: What is that over the head and under the hat?

text: If you drop me I'm sure to crack, but give me a smile and I'll never smile back. I hold your photograph. What am I?
why_original_fails: A mirror smiles back; the thing that never smiles back and holds a photograph is a picture frame.
original_text: If you drop me I'm sure to crack. But give me a smile and I'll always smile back.

text: The eight of us move forth and back, to protect our king from the foe's attack. Which piece do we protect?
why_original_fails: The question asks which piece is protected, the king; 'pawns' are the speakers.
original_text: The eight of us move forth and back. To protect our king from the foes attack.

text: By day I come without being fetched. At night I am lost without being stolen. What am I?
why_original_fails: Night and day are swapped, so the thing that comes by day and is lost at night is the sun, not the stars.
original_text: At night I come without being fetched. By day I am lost without being stolen.

text: I'm very tempting, so it's said. I have a shiny coat of red, and my flesh is white beneath. I am a root, pulled from the ground. What am I?
why_original_fails: An apple grows on a tree; a red-skinned, white-fleshed root pulled from the ground is a radish.
original_text: I'm very tempting, so its said, I have a shiny coat of red, and my flesh is white beneath. I smell so sweet, taste good to eat, and help to guard your teeth.

text: I have feathers to help me fly. I have a body and head, but I'm not alive. It is your strength which determines how far I go. You hold me in your hand, and then you throw me. What am I?
why_original_fails: An arrow is never thrown, it is shot; a feathered thing thrown by hand is a dart.
original_text: I have many feathers to help me fly. I have a body and head, but I'm not alive. It is your strength which determines how far I go. You can hold me in your hand, but I'm never thrown.

text: I sleep by day, I fly by night. I have feathers to aid my flight. What am I?
why_original_fails: A bat has no feathers; a nocturnal flier with feathers is an owl.
original_text: I sleep by day, I fly by night. I have no feathers to aid my flight.

text: Charcoal is black when you get it, red when you use it, and white when you're all through with it. What color is it while you are using it?
why_original_fails: The question asks for a color during use, which the text gives as red; 'charcoal' is stated, not asked.
original_text: What's black when you get it, red when you use it, and white when you're all through with it?

text: A slow, solemn square-dance of warriors feinting. One by one they fall, warriors fainting, twenty-four on sixty-four. What is it?
why_original_fails: Chess has thirty-two pieces; twenty-four pieces on sixty-four squares is checkers.
original_text: A slow, solemn square-dance of warriors feinting. One by one they fall, warriors fainting, thirty-two on sixty-four.

text: This thing runs but cannot walk, sometimes sings but never talks. Lacks arms, has hands; lacks a head but has a face; and it is strapped to your wrist. What is it?
why_original_fails: A clock is not strapped to a wrist; a watch is.
original_text: This thing runs but cannot walk, sometimes sings but never talks. Lacks arms, has hands; lacks a head but has a face.

text: A box with hinges, lock and key, and golden treasure lies within. What is it?
why_original_fails: An egg has no hinges, lock or key; a box that has all three and holds treasure is a treasure chest.
original_text: A box without hinges, lock or key, yet golden treasure lies within.

text: What is pronounced like one letter, written with three letters, and is a hot drink?
why_original_fails: 'Eye' is not a drink; 'tea' is pronounced like the letter T, has three letters, and is a hot drink.
original_text: What is pronounced like one letter, written with three letters. And belongs to all animals?

text: They have flesh and bone, and skin of their own. They have fingers and thumbs, and are on the ends of your arms. What are they?
why_original_fails: Gloves have no flesh or bone; hands have both and end the arms.
original_text: They have not flesh, nor feathers, nor scales, nor bone. Yet they have fingers and thumbs of their own.

text: What goes into the boiling water dark and comes out red?
why_original_fails: Iron goes in red and comes out dark; a lobster goes in dark and comes out red.
original_text: What goes in the water red, and comes out black?

text: An iron horse with a flaxen tail. The faster the horse runs, the shorter his tail becomes. What is the tail?
why_original_fails: The question asks about the tail, which is the thread; 'needle' is the horse.
original_text: An iron horse with a flaxen tail. The faster the horse runs, the shorter his tail becomes.

text: Take off my skin, I won't cry, and neither will you. I am yellow and curved. What am I?
why_original_fails: Peeling an onion makes you cry; a yellow, curved fruit peeled without tears is a banana.
original_text: Take off my skin, I won't cry, but you will.

text: He has married many couples but has never married himself. He wears a robe and presides over a courtroom. Who is he?
why_original_fails: A priest does not preside over a courtroom; a judge does and can officiate marriages.
original_text: He has married many women but has never married.

text: A beggar's sister went out to sea and drowned. But the woman who drowned had no sister. Who was the beggar to the woman who drowned?
why_original_fails: The sexes are swapped: the drowned woman had no sister, so the beggar is her brother.
original_text: A beggar's brother went out to sea and drowned. But the man who drowned had no brother. Who was the beggar to the man who drowned?

text: Eighty-eight horses, black and white, on a wooden hill. First they sound, then they sing, then they stand still. What are they?
why_original_fails: Teeth are thirty-two and white on a red hill; eighty-eight black and white keys on wood are a piano's.
original_text: Thirty white horses on a red hill, First they champ, Then they stamp, Then they stand still.

jalapeno:DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731.final: The 88 black-and-white keys of a piano
jalapeno:DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731.label: correct

text: The cloud is my mother. The wind is my father. I have a million brothers. I die when I reach the ground. What am I?
why_original_fails: A wave is born of the sea and dies on land; something born of a cloud that dies on the ground is a raindrop.
original_text: The moon is my father. The sea is my mother. I have a million brothers. I die when I reach land.

text: I have two wings and I do fly. I never laugh and never cry. I carry people through the sky. What am I?
why_original_fails: A windmill has four wings and cannot fly; a two-winged flier that carries people is an airplane.
original_text: I have four wings but cannot fly. I never laugh and never cry. On the same spot always found, toiling away with little sound.

text: You see me once in July, twice in August, and not at all in May. What am I?
why_original_fails: 'July' has one U, 'August' two, 'May' none; N appears in none of these months.
original_text: You see me once in June, twice in November, and not at all in May. What am I?

text: What gets wetter the more it dries, has a long handle, and a soft head you push across the floor?
why_original_fails: A towel has no handle and is not pushed across a floor; a mop has both and gets wetter as it dries the floor.
original_text: What gets wetter the more it dries?

text: A towel gets wetter the more it dries. A sponge, on the other hand, gets lighter the more it dries. What gets lighter the more it dries?
why_original_fails: The text says the sponge gets lighter; the question asks about that, not about what gets wetter.
original_text: What gets wetter the more it dries?

text: The more you take, the more you leave behind. Each one is about 75 centimetres long for an adult. Roughly how many do you leave behind walking 750 metres?
why_original_fails: The question asks for a count (750 m / 0.75 m = 1,000), not for what the things are.
original_text: The more you take, the more you leave behind. What am I?

text: I speak without a mouth and hear without ears. I have a body with a cord, and I come alive when I ring. What am I?
why_original_fails: An echo has no body, no cord, and does not ring; a corded telephone speaks, hears, and rings.
original_text: I speak without a mouth and hear without ears. I have no body, but I come alive with wind. What am I?

text: What has a head, a tail, is silver, has no legs, and is worth ten cents?
why_original_fails: A penny is brown and worth one cent; the coin worth ten cents is a dime.
original_text: What has a head, a tail, is brown, and has no legs?

text: What has a head, a tail, is brown, has no legs, lives in the soil, and is eaten by birds?
why_original_fails: A penny does not live in soil or get eaten by birds; an earthworm has a head and tail, is brown, legless, lives in soil and is eaten by birds.
original_text: What has a head, a tail, is brown, and has no legs?

text: A river runs but never walks, has a mouth but never talks, has a head but never weeps, has a bed but never sleeps. Which of these parts does a person also have and use to talk?
why_original_fails: The question asks which named part a person talks with; 'a river' answers the wrong question.
original_text: What runs but never walks, has a mouth but never talks, has a head but never weeps, has a bed but never sleeps?

text: What goes up in the east and comes down in the west every day, and is too bright to look at directly?
why_original_fails: Your age never comes down; the sun rises in the east, sets in the west daily, and is too bright to look at (the moon is not).
original_text: What goes up but never comes down?

text: "Silence is so fragile that saying its name breaks it," said the teacher, "and a secret is so fragile that telling it ends it." According to the teacher, what is so fragile that telling it ends it?
why_original_fails: The teacher's second sentence names the secret; silence answers the first sentence, which is not what is asked.
original_text: What is so fragile that saying its name breaks it?

text: What is always behind you, can never be seen again, and grows longer every day you live?
why_original_fails: The future is in front of you, not behind; what is behind you, never seen again, and grows every day is the past (your back does not grow).
original_text: What is always in front of you but can't be seen?

text: What is always in front of you but can't be seen, and you breathe it?
why_original_fails: You cannot breathe the future; air is invisible, always in front of you, and breathed.
original_text: What is always in front of you but can't be seen?

text: What belongs to you, is used by other people more than by you, and is a string of digits they dial?
why_original_fails: A name is not a string of digits that is dialled; a phone number is.
original_text: What belongs to you, but other people use it more than you do?

text: I am light as a feather, and even a child can hold me for hours without effort, but I float away if they let go of my string. What am I?
why_original_fails: Breath cannot be held for hours; a helium balloon on a string can, and floats away when released.
original_text: I am light as a feather, yet the strongest man can't hold me for more than a few minutes. What am I?

text: An elephant's shadow is as big as an elephant but weighs nothing. What is exactly as big as that shadow and weighs about five tonnes?
why_original_fails: The shadow weighs nothing; the five-tonne thing of the same size is the elephant.
original_text: What is as big as an elephant but weighs nothing?

text: I am not alive, but I grow; I don't have lungs, but I need air; I don't have a mouth, and water makes me grow faster. I turn iron orange-brown. What am I?
why_original_fails: Water kills fire; rust needs air and water, grows, and turns iron orange-brown.
original_text: I am not alive, but I grow; I don't have lungs, but I need air; I don't have a mouth, but water kills me. What am I?

text: What starts with an E, ends with an E, contains only one letter, and is the fifth letter of the alphabet?
why_original_fails: An envelope is not the fifth letter of the alphabet; the letter E starts and ends with E, is one letter, and is fifth.
original_text: What starts with an E, ends with an E, but only contains one letter?

text: I am the beginning of night, the end of noon, and I appear twice in nine. What am I?
why_original_fails: E does not begin 'night' or end 'noon'; N does both and appears twice in 'nine'.
original_text: I am the beginning of the end, and the end of time and space. I am essential to creation, and I surround every place. What am I?

text: I am the beginning of the end, and the end of time and space. I am essential to creation, and I surround every place. How many times do I appear in the word 'excellence'?
why_original_fails: The question asks for a count; 'the letter E' is the thing counted, not the count (e-x-c-e-l-l-e-n-c-e has four Es).
original_text: I am the beginning of the end, and the end of time and space. I am essential to creation, and I surround every place. What am I?

text: What letter is at the beginning of everything and at the end of time?
why_original_fails: G is at the end of 'everything', not the beginning; E begins 'everything' and ends 'time'.
original_text: What is at the end of everything?

text: What letter is at the beginning of March and May but not in April?
why_original_fails: R is in the middle of March and April; the letter that begins March and May and is absent from April is M.
original_text: What is seen in the middle of March and April that can't be seen at the beginning or end of either month?

text: What letter is at the beginning of a rainbow and at the end of a river?
why_original_fails: W is at the end of 'rainbow'; R begins 'rainbow' and ends 'river'.
original_text: What is at the end of a rainbow?

text: What room has no doors or windows, and you sweep the floor with it?
why_original_fails: You do not sweep with a mushroom; a broom contains 'room' and sweeps floors.
original_text: What room has no doors or windows?

text: What room has no doors or windows, and marries the bride?
why_original_fails: A mushroom does not marry anyone; the groom contains 'room' and marries the bride.
original_text: What room has no doors or windows?

jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.final: The groom (it contains "room" and marries the bride)
jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.label: correct

text: What is full of holes, cannot hold water, and you drain pasta with it?
why_original_fails: A sponge holds water; the holed thing that lets water through and drains pasta is a colander.
original_text: What is full of holes but still holds water?

text: What arrived exactly one day ago and is never coming again?
why_original_fails: Tomorrow never arrives; what arrived exactly a day ago and will never come again is yesterday.
original_text: What is always coming but never arrives?

text: What has ears but cannot hear, is stuffed with cotton, and is given to children to cuddle?
why_original_fails: Corn is not stuffed with cotton or cuddled; a teddy bear has ears, cannot hear, and is.
original_text: What has ears but cannot hear?

text: A stamp travels around the world but stays in a corner. In which corner of the envelope does it stay?
why_original_fails: The question asks which corner; 'a stamp' is the thing, not the corner.
original_text: What travels around the world but stays in a corner?

text: What travels around the world but stays in one place, circling 400 kilometres up every 90 minutes with astronauts aboard?
why_original_fails: A stamp does not orbit with astronauts; the ISS circles the Earth at about 400 km every 90 minutes.
original_text: What travels around the world but stays in a corner?

text: What can you keep after giving it to someone, and it makes both of you sneeze and cough for a week?
why_original_fails: Your word does not make anyone sneeze; a cold is kept after being passed on and makes both people sneeze and cough for a week (pepper does not last a week).
original_text: What can you keep after giving it to someone?

text: In the dictionary, today comes before yesterday. Which of the two comes first on a calendar?
why_original_fails: The question asks which day comes first in time; 'in the dictionary' answers where, not which.
original_text: Where does today come before yesterday?

text: The one who makes it doesn't use it. The one who buys it doesn't use it. The one who uses it is a baby, wets it, and doesn't know it. What is it?
why_original_fails: A coffin is not used by a baby who wets it; a diaper is.
original_text: The man who makes it doesn't want it. The man who buys it doesn't use it. The man who uses it doesn't know it. What is it?

text: The man who makes a coffin doesn't want it. The man who buys it doesn't use it. Who uses it?
why_original_fails: The question asks who uses the coffin; 'a coffin' is the object, not the user.
original_text: The man who makes it doesn't want it. The man who buys it doesn't use it. The man who uses it doesn't know it. What is it?

text: What has a spine and bones, no legs, and breathes through gills?
why_original_fails: A book has no bones and no gills; a fish (or a tadpole) has a spine, bones, no legs, and gills.
original_text: What has a spine but no bones?

text: You can see me in water, but I never get wet, and I am 384,000 kilometres away and shine at night. What am I?
why_original_fails: A reflection is not 384,000 km away; the moon is, is seen in water, and never gets wet.
original_text: You can see me in water, but I never get wet. What am I?

text: You can see me in water, I am always wet, I have fins and scales, and I breathe through gills. What am I?
why_original_fails: A reflection never gets wet and has no fins, scales or gills; a fish has all three and is always wet.
original_text: You can see me in water, but I never get wet. What am I?

text: What is green when you buy it, red when it ripens, and is the base of ketchup?
why_original_fails: Charcoal is never green and is not the base of ketchup; a tomato ripens from green to red and is.
original_text: What is black when you buy it, red when you use it, and gray when you throw it away?

text: Charcoal is black when you buy it, red when you use it, and gray when you throw it away. What colour is it while it is burning?
why_original_fails: The question asks for a colour; 'charcoal' is the thing, and the text says it is red when used.
original_text: What is black when you buy it, red when you use it, and gray when you throw it away?

text: What has one head, four feet, four legs, and barks?
why_original_fails: A bed has one foot and does not bark; a dog has four feet and barks.
original_text: What has one head, one foot, and four legs?

text: A bed has one head, one foot, and four legs. How many feet does it have?
why_original_fails: The question asks for the number of feet stated in the text; 'a bed' answers the wrong question.
original_text: What has one head, one foot, and four legs?

text: I am white when I am clean and black when I am dirty, and you write on me with a marker. What am I?
why_original_fails: A chalkboard is black when clean and takes chalk; a whiteboard is white when clean and takes a marker.
original_text: I am black when I am clean and white when I am dirty. What am I?

text: What starts with T, ends with T, and you sleep in it when camping?
why_original_fails: Nobody sleeps in a teapot; a tent starts and ends with T and is slept in when camping.
original_text: What starts with T, ends with T, and has T in it?

text: What starts with T, ends with T, has T in it, and is a sweet pastry filled with fruit?
why_original_fails: A teapot is not a pastry; a tart starts and ends with T, has a T in it, and is a fruit pastry.
original_text: What starts with T, ends with T, and has T in it?

text: What has a tongue and can pant, gets around a lot and can walk, and barks?
why_original_fails: A shoe cannot walk or bark; a dog has a tongue, pants, walks, and barks.
original_text: What has a tongue but cannot talk, gets around a lot but cannot walk?

text: What has three hearts, no bones, eight arms, and lives in the sea?
why_original_fails: A deck of cards has thirteen hearts and no arms; an octopus has three hearts, no bones, eight arms, and lives in the sea.
original_text: What has 13 hearts but no other organs?

text: A standard deck of 52 cards has 13 hearts but no other organs. How many cards in the deck are of suits other than hearts?
why_original_fails: The question asks for a count (52 minus 13); 'a deck of cards' is not a count.
original_text: What has 13 hearts but no other organs?

text: What building has the most storeys, counting only floors, with 163 of them, in Dubai?
why_original_fails: The pun on stories is removed: counting floors, the 163-floor building in Dubai is the Burj Khalifa, not a library.
original_text: What building has the most stories?

text: What building has the fewest stories, just one, and is where a farmer keeps hay and cows?
why_original_fails: A library has the most stories; the single-storey farm building for hay and cows is a barn.
original_text: What building has the most stories?

text: The word 'wrong' is spelled w-r-o-n-g in every dictionary. What word is spelled r-i-g-h-t in every dictionary?
why_original_fails: The question spells out r-i-g-h-t; 'wrong' is the other word in the text.
original_text: What word is spelled wrong in every dictionary?

text: What invention lets a doctor look right through your skin to your bones?
why_original_fails: A window does not show bones through skin; an X-ray does.
original_text: What invention lets you look right through a wall?

text: What has wheels and flies, is an aircraft, and takes off from a runway?
why_original_fails: The original excludes aircraft; this text says it is an aircraft that takes off from a runway, so it is an airplane, not a garbage truck.
original_text: What has wheels and flies but is not an aircraft?

text: What has a heart that doesn't beat, is a leafy green, and is the base of a Caesar salad?
why_original_fails: An artichoke is not the leafy base of a Caesar salad; romaine lettuce has a heart and is.
original_text: What has a heart that doesn't beat?

text: What goes up and down stairs without moving, and is the rail you hold on to?
why_original_fails: A carpet is not held; the rail you hold that runs up and down the stairs is the banister.
original_text: What goes up and down stairs without moving?

text: The word 'alphabet' contains 26 letters but only three syllables. How many letters does the word 'alphabet' itself have when you spell it?
why_original_fails: The question asks for the letter count of the word (a-l-p-h-a-b-e-t = 8); 'alphabet' is the word, not the count.
original_text: What word contains 26 letters but only has three syllables?

text: What has lots of eyes and sees with all of them, has eight legs, and spins a web?
why_original_fails: A potato's eyes cannot see and it has no legs; a spider has many seeing eyes, eight legs, and spins webs.
original_text: What has lots of eyes but can't see?

text: What kind of tree can you carry in your hands, is about 30 centimetres tall, and is grown in a shallow pot in Japan?
why_original_fails: The pun on palm is removed: a real tree small enough to carry, grown in a shallow pot in Japan, is a bonsai.
original_text: What kind of tree can you carry in your hand?

text: A bear with no teeth is called a gummy bear. What do you call a bear that is white and lives in the Arctic?
why_original_fails: The question asks about the white Arctic bear, which is a polar bear; the gummy bear is only mentioned.
original_text: What do you call a bear with no teeth?

text: A cat's left side has been shaved for surgery and its right side has not. Which side of the cat has the most fur?
why_original_fails: The text fixes one shaved side, so the answer is the unshaved right side, not 'the outside'.
original_text: Which side of a cat has the most fur?

text: Which can jump higher: a flea or a building?
why_original_fails: The question offers two choices; the joke answer 'anything, buildings can't jump' is not one of them, and the flea is the one that jumps.
original_text: What can jump higher than a building?

text: What has twelve faces but does not wear makeup, and forty-two eyes but cannot see?
why_original_fails: One die has six faces and twenty-one eyes; twelve faces and forty-two eyes is two dice.
original_text: What has six faces but does not wear makeup, and twenty-one eyes but cannot see?

text: A die has six faces and twenty-one eyes, and its opposite faces always add up to seven. How many eyes are on the face opposite the six?
why_original_fails: The question asks for a number (7 minus 6); 'a die' answers the wrong question.
original_text: What has six faces but does not wear makeup, and twenty-one eyes but cannot see?

text: What can you serve but never eat, and it is handed down by a judge?
why_original_fails: A judge does not hand down tennis balls; a prison sentence is served and never eaten.
original_text: What can you serve but never eat?

text: What is orange, grows on a tree, and has the same name as its colour?
why_original_fails: A carrot grows underground and is not named after its colour; an orange is.
original_text: What is orange and sounds like a parrot?

text: A carrot is orange and sounds like a parrot. What sounds like 'carrot' and measures the purity of gold?
why_original_fails: The question asks for the gold-purity word that sounds like carrot: karat; the carrot is only mentioned.
original_text: What is orange and sounds like a parrot?

text: What is golden-brown and sticky, made by bees, and spread on toast?
why_original_fails: A stick is not made by bees or spread on toast; honey is brown, sticky, made by bees, and spread on toast.
original_text: What is brown and sticky?

text: A stick is brown and sticky. What is white and sticky, and comes in a bottle for gluing paper?
why_original_fails: The question asks for the white sticky thing in a bottle for paper: glue; the stick is only mentioned.
original_text: What is brown and sticky?

text: I shear every day, but my own coat stays the same, because I only shear sheep. What am I?
why_original_fails: A barber shaves people, not sheep; the person who shears sheep daily is a shearer.
original_text: I shave every day, but my beard stays the same. What am I?

text: A barber shaves every day, but his beard stays the same. Whose beards does he shave?

text: What can be cracked, scrambled, boiled, and fried, and is laid by a hen?

original_text: What can be cracked, made, told, and played?

text: What can be cracked, picked, and broken, and keeps a door shut?

text: What is hard to get into but easy to get out of, and has a bouncer at the door?

original_text: What is easy to get into but hard to get out of?

text: What can you put in a bucket to make it weigh more, and it falls from the sky?

original_text: What can you put in a bucket to make it weigh less?

text: The word 'queue' is pronounced the same if you take away four of its five letters. Which letter is left?
why_original_fails: The question asks which letter remains; 'queue' is the word, not the remaining letter.
original_text: What word is pronounced the same if you take away four of its five letters?

text: I have no life, but I can die, and I have six faces marked with one to six dots. What am I?

original_text: I have no life, but I can die. What am I?

text: I have a life, and they say I have nine of them, and I purr. What am I?
why_original_fails: A battery has no life and does not purr; a cat has nine lives, they say, and purrs.
original_text: I have no life, but I can die. What am I?

text: The word 'bookkeeper' has three consecutive double letters. Which three letters are doubled?
why_original_fails: The question asks which letters are doubled; 'bookkeeper' is the word, not the letters.
original_text: What English word has three consecutive double letters?

text: What is made almost entirely of water, lives in water, dies if you take it out of water, and has no brain, no bones, and a sting?
why_original_fails: An ice cube dies in water; a jellyfish is mostly water, lives in it, dies out of it, and stings.
original_text: What is made of water but if you put it into water it will die?

text: You can never eat lunch or dinner for breakfast. Which of the three meals do you eat in the morning?
why_original_fails: The question asks for the morning meal; 'lunch and dinner' are the meals that are not it.
original_text: What can you never eat for breakfast?

text: Adding a G to the front of 'one' makes it 'gone'. What word do you get by adding a B to the front of 'one'?

original_text: How do you make the number one disappear?
original_answer: add a G and it's gone

text: What is black and white and red all over, blushing after eating too much bamboo?
why_original_fails: 'Red' here is the colour, not 'read', and a newspaper does not eat bamboo; a blushing panda is black, white, and red.
original_text: What is black and white and read all over?

text: What is black and white and has 88 keys?
why_original_fails: A newspaper has no keys; a piano is black and white and has 88 keys.
original_text: What is black and white and read all over?

text: A plane crashes exactly on the border between the United States and Canada. There are no survivors: the only two passengers, both Canadian citizens, died, and their families asked for them to be buried in their home country. In which country are they buried?
why_original_fails: The text already says there are no survivors and states where the dead are buried; 'you don't bury survivors' answers a question the text no longer asks.
original_text: A plane crashes exactly on the border between the United States and Canada. Where do they bury the survivors?

text: Before Mount Everest was measured in 1856, surveyors believed Kangchenjunga was the highest mountain in the world. Before 1856, which mountain did surveyors believe was the highest?

original_text: Before Mount Everest was discovered, what was the highest mountain in the world?

text: A woman was born on February 29th and has celebrated exactly 20 birthdays on that date. To the nearest ten years, how old is she?

original_text: A man died of old age on his 25th birthday. How is this possible?

text: A cowboy rides into town on Monday morning, stays in town all of Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, and leaves the next morning on his horse, whose name is Friday. On which day of the week does he leave?

original_text: A cowboy rides into town on Friday, stays for three days, and leaves on Friday. How is that possible?

text: A man pushes his car to a hotel and tells the owner he is bankrupt, because he is playing Monopoly. What is the car?
why_original_fails: The text states he is playing Monopoly and asks what the car is; 'he is playing Monopoly' answers the wrong question.
original_text: A man pushes his car to a hotel and tells the owner he is bankrupt. Why?

text: Almost everyone needs it, asks for it, takes it, and pays it back with interest. What is it?
why_original_fails: Advice is not paid back with interest; a loan is asked for, taken, and repaid with interest.
original_text: Almost everyone needs it, asks for it, gives it. But almost nobody takes it.

text: I am seen in a stop sign, a ripe tomato, a ruby, and the top stripe of the rainbow. What colour am I?
why_original_fails: Blue is not the colour of a stop sign, a ripe tomato, a ruby, or the rainbow's top stripe; red is.
original_text: I am seen in the water. If seen in the sky, I am in the rainbow, a jay's feather, and lapis lazuli.

text: I have four legs but walk not, a flat top but no back and no arms, and you eat your dinner off me. What am I?
why_original_fails: A chair has a back and a seat; the four-legged thing with a flat top, no back, and dinner on it is a table.
original_text: I have legs but walk not, a strong back but work not. Two good arms but reach not. A seat but sit and tarry not.

text: What is put on a table, cut, and eaten at a birthday party with candles on top?
why_original_fails: A deck of cards is never eaten and has no candles; a birthday cake is cut and eaten with candles on top.
original_text: What is put on a table, cut, but never eaten?

text: A dentist digs out tiny caves and stores gold and silver in them, and builds bridges of silver and crowns of gold. Where are these tiny caves?
why_original_fails: The question asks where the caves are; 'a dentist' is who digs them, not where.
original_text: I dig out tiny caves and store gold and silver in them. I also build bridges of silver and make crowns of gold. They are the smallest you could imagine. Sooner or later everybody needs my help. Yet many people are afraid to let me help them.

text: An elephant has a face with a tree, skin like the sea, a great beast, yet vermin frightens it. What is the 'tree' on its face?
why_original_fails: The question asks about the part called a tree; 'an elephant' is the whole animal.
original_text: Face with a tree, skin like the sea. A great beast I am. Yet vermin frightens me.

text: Who spends the day at the window, goes to the table for meals, hides at night, purrs, and has whiskers?
why_original_fails: A fly does not purr or have whiskers; a cat does.
original_text: Who spends the day at the window, goes to the table for meals. And hides at night?

text: What do you fill with empty feet and then lace up?
why_original_fails: Gloves are filled with hands, not feet, and have no laces; shoes are filled with feet and laced up.
original_text: What do you fill with empty hands?

text: The sun bakes them, the hand breaks them, the foot treads on them, and the mouth tastes them. What drink do the trodden ones become?
why_original_fails: The question asks what the trodden grapes become; 'grapes' is what they are.
original_text: The sun bakes them, the hand breaks them, the foot treads on them, and the mouth tastes them.

text: A key: what force and strength cannot get through, it can with a gentle touch. What does it open?
why_original_fails: The question asks what the key opens; 'a key' is the opener.
original_text: What force and strength cannot get through. I, with a gentle touch, can do. Many in the street would stand. Were I not a friend at hand.

text: I'm never white and always right. I can hurt to hear but I set you free, they say. What am I?
why_original_fails: A lie is sometimes white and always wrong; what is always right and sets you free is the truth.
original_text: I'm sometimes white and always wrong. I can break a heart and hurt the strong. I can build love or tear it down. I can make a smile or bring a frown.

text: The moon is always old, sometimes new, sometimes blue, sometimes full, and never pushes but always pulls. What does it pull on the Earth, twice a day?
why_original_fails: The question asks what the moon pulls; 'the moon' is the puller.
original_text: Always old, sometimes new. Never sad, sometimes blue. Never empty, sometimes full. Never pushes, always pulls.

jalapeno:DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731.final: It doesn’t pull anything twice a day—its gravitational pull is continuous; tides are the twice-daily effect.

text: At the sound of me, one may dream or stamp their feet. At the sound of me, everyone in the building must leave at once because there may be a fire. What am I?
why_original_fails: Music does not make everyone leave a building at once; a fire alarm does.
original_text: At the sound of me, one may dream or stamp their feet, At the sound of me, one may laugh or sometimes weep.

text: You use a knife to slice my head, and you smile, because I am sweet and red with black seeds throughout. What am I?
why_original_fails: An onion makes you weep and is not sweet; a watermelon is sweet, red, and full of black seeds.
original_text: You use a knife to slice my head. And weep beside me when I am dead.

text: I wear a yellow coat with black stripes, I buzz from flower to flower, and I make honey. What am I?
why_original_fails: A pencil does not buzz or make honey; a bee is yellow and black, buzzes, and makes honey.
original_text: I usually wear a yellow coat. I usually have a dark head. I make marks wherever I go.

text: Sand builds up castles, tears down mountains, makes some men blind, and helps others to see. What is made from sand that helps people see?
why_original_fails: The question asks what sand is made into; 'sand' is the raw material.
original_text: I build up castles. I tear down mountains. I make some men blind. I help others to see.

jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.final: Glass — used to make eyeglass lenses
jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.label: correct

text: What has a neck and no head, two arms but no hands, and a hook on top so it can hang in a wardrobe holding a shirt?
why_original_fails: A shirt has no hook and does not hold a shirt; a coat hanger has a neck, two arms, a hook, and holds a shirt.
original_text: What has a neck and no head, two arms but no hands?

text: Sleep weakens all men for hours each day and shows them strange visions while they are away. What are the strange visions called?
why_original_fails: The question asks what the visions are called; 'sleep' is the state that brings them.
original_text: I weaken all men for hours each day. I show you strange visions while you are away. I take you by night, by day take you back. None suffer to have me, but do from my lack.

text: I carry no house on my back and have no shell at all, yet I am not rich and leave silver in my track. What am I?
why_original_fails: A snail carries its shell; the shell-less creature that leaves a silver trail is a slug.
original_text: If a man carried my burden, he would break his back. I am not rich, but leave silver in my track.

text: Who is she that walks on four legs, with her house on her back, and can live for a hundred years?
why_original_fails: A snail has no legs; the four-legged creature with a house on its back that lives a century is a tortoise.
original_text: Who is he that runs without a leg. And his house on his back?

text: I saw a man in white, not old, standing in the cold. When he felt the sun he did not move at all, because he is carved from marble. Who could he be?
why_original_fails: A snowman runs (melts) in the sun; a marble statue stays exactly as it is.
original_text: I saw a man in white, he looked quite a sight. He was not old, but he stood in the cold. And when he felt the sun, he started to run. Who could he be? Please answer me.

text: I move without wings, between silken string, and I spin a cocoon and turn into a moth. What am I?
why_original_fails: A spider never becomes a moth; a silkworm spins silk, makes a cocoon, and turns into a moth.
original_text: I move without wings, Between silken string, I leave as you find, My substance behind.

text: Water has three lives: gentle enough to soothe the skin, light enough to caress the sky, hard enough to crack rocks. Which of its three forms is the one hard enough to crack rocks?
why_original_fails: The question asks which form of water is hard; 'water' is the substance, not the form.
original_text: Three lives have I. Gentle enough to soothe the skin. Light enough to caress the sky. Hard enough to crack rocks.

text: As round as an apple, as deep as a cup, and every morning a rope pulls it up full of water from the well. What is it?
why_original_fails: A well cannot be pulled up; the thing pulled up from a well full of water is a bucket.
original_text: As round as an apple. As deep as a cup. All the king's horses can't pull it up.

text: When young, wine is sweet in the sun; when middle-aged, it makes you gay; when old, it is valued more than ever. What fruit is it made from?
why_original_fails: The question asks about the fruit; 'wine' is what the fruit becomes.
original_text: When young, I am sweet in the sun. When middle-aged, I make you gay. When old, I am valued more than ever.

text: I am an even number. Take away a letter and I become a word meaning 'in the direction of'. What number am I?
why_original_fails: Seven is odd; the even number that becomes 'to' when a letter is removed is two.
original_text: I am an odd number. Take away a letter and I become even. What number am I?

text: What gets duller the more you use it, is made of steel, and has a handle?
why_original_fails: A brain gets sharper with use and is not steel; a steel knife with a handle gets duller with use.
original_text: What gets sharper the more you use it?

text: A saucepan's lid can't be put in the saucepan. Where does the lid go instead?
why_original_fails: The question asks where the lid goes; 'its lid' is the thing, not the place.
original_text: What can't be put in a saucepan?

original_text: A man builds a house with all four sides facing south. A bear walks by. What colour is the bear?

text: A man builds a house with all four sides facing north. Where must the house be?

original_text: A man builds a house with all four sides facing south. A bear walks by. What colour is the bear?

text: If you drop a red stone into a bucket of white paint, what colour will it be when you pull it out?
why_original_fails: The stone is coated in white paint, so the answer is a colour; 'wet' is the sea-riddle pun the text no longer supports.
original_text: If you throw a red stone into the blue sea, what will it become?

text: A man can go eight days without sleep by sleeping at night. How can a night-shift worker go eight nights without sleeping at night?
why_original_fails: The question is the mirror of the original; 'he sleeps at night' is the case the question rules out.

original_text: What is at the center of gravity?

text: What starts with A, ends with T, and has 26 letters?
why_original_fails: The post office starts with P and ends with E; what starts with A, ends with T, and has 26 letters is the alphabet.
original_text: What starts with P, ends with E, and has thousands of letters?

text: Ten stone statues of birds sit on a wire. A hunter shoots one and it shatters. How many statues are left on the wire?
why_original_fails: Stone statues cannot fly away, so nine remain; 'none' is the memorized answer for live birds.
original_text: Ten birds are sitting on a wire. A hunter shoots one. How many are left?

text: Ten birds are sitting on a wire. A hunter shoots one and the rest fly away. How many birds flew away?
why_original_fails: The question asks how many flew away (ten minus the one shot), not how many are left.
original_text: Ten birds are sitting on a wire. A hunter shoots one. How many are left?
